overview: The Cooperative Watershed Management Program, run by the Interior Department's Bureau of Reclamation, gives grants to local groups that bring together water users, landowners, and others to manage a shared watershed, the land area that drains into a river or stream. This bill renews the program, authorizing $20 million a year from 2027 through 2031. It raises the cap on first-phase grants for forming and organizing these groups from $100,000 to $150,000 and allows up to two more years of funding for groups that perform well. It makes groups facing drought, wildfire, or other disasters eligible, counts tribes with ancestral lands in a watershed as stakeholders, and lets grants pay for grant writing, project management, engineering, and monitoring results after construction. It also requires the department to accept applications several times a year and make its program reports public. As of September 17, 2026, a Senate committee had approved it with changes and it was placed on the Senate calendar for possible floor action.
for: Supporters say locally led watershed groups are a low-cost way to resolve water conflicts and plan projects, and the changes help smaller and disaster-hit communities take part.
against: Critics say the bill expands a federal grant program and its eligible costs, and that funding staff and planning work could take money away from projects that actually deliver water.
